overview: This atlas record is a failed historical-basemap hypothesis, not a documented “Proto-Thai civilization.” Proto-Tai is reconstructed by comparing later Tai languages; it is not an attested self-name, state, ethnicity, or archaeological culture. The lone 400 to 323 BCE polygon conflicts with scholarship. Its twenty-seven-position ring spans roughly 102.6 to 127.0 degrees east and 34.4 to 44.2 degrees north. Lanzhou and Ordos test inside, while Nanning, Guangzhou, Guiyang, Hanoi, and every sampled southern city test outside. Precision matters here. Kra-Dai diversity and most homeland proposals instead point toward southern China, though routes and dates remain debated. Regional archaeology documents rice, fishing, pottery, bronze, weaving, settlement, and exchange, but cannot tie all remains to Proto-Tai speakers. Comparative reconstruction supports *tamᴮ “weave”; the asterisk marks a modern inference, not ancient writing. No Proto-Tai inscription or sentence survives from this interval. The 323 BCE endpoint is an atlas repaint, not a fall, migration, or extinction. Later Tai languages, scripts, societies, and living communities have distinct histories.

periods.title: An atlas label appears far north of the linguistic evidence
periods.summary: The map introduces one “Proto-Thai cultures” polygon, but it covers a diagonal slice of north China rather than the southern regions discussed in Kra-Dai scholarship. This ten-year division is editorial: neither comparative linguistics nor archaeology identifies a Proto-Tai state, migration, or cultural founding in 400 BCE.

periods.title: Comparative reconstruction is evidence, not a census
periods.summary: Proto-Tai is reconstructed by comparing later Tai languages and separating inheritance from borrowing, convergence, and parallel change. That method can recover sound systems and vocabulary. It cannot name every speaker, draw a political border, or make all people inside an atlas polygon members of one ethnicity.

periods.title: Kra-Dai diversity points south, with uncertainty attached
periods.summary: Modern Kra-Dai diversity is concentrated in southern China and mainland Southeast Asia. Phylogenetic and geographic studies propose different homelands and dispersal routes, with wide chronological uncertainty. None validates this map’s north-China geometry or pins Proto-Tai’s breakup to this particular decade.

periods.title: Archaeology records communities without language labels
periods.summary: Southern China and mainland Southeast Asia preserve farming, pottery, bronze, iron, weaving, exchange, settlement, and burial evidence. Archaeological cultures are patterns in things, not recordings of speech. Researchers cannot securely attach every Lingnan or Dong Son object to Proto-Tai people merely because later Tai languages exist nearby.

periods.title: Reconstructed words suggest skills, not one uniform culture
periods.summary: A reconstructible Proto-Tai verb for weaving supports knowledge of the activity among ancestral speakers. It does not reveal a single loom design, household division of labor, cloth style, or archaeological population. Technologies can travel across language boundaries, while people can change language and keep tools.

periods.title: Rice, rivers, and trade remain regional evidence
periods.summary: Rice cultivation and river or coastal exchange shaped many southern communities, including speakers of several language families. Crop remains, boats, ceramics, and traded bronzes illuminate regional lifeways. They cannot identify speech without an independent link, so the card treats “Proto-Tai rice culture” as a hypothesis requiring proof.

periods.title: Writing remains unattested for the proposed subject
periods.summary: No reviewed source supplies a securely dated Proto-Tai inscription or native sentence from 400 to 323 BCE. A reconstruction such as *tamᴮ “weave” is a modern scholarly notation built from daughter languages, not ancient handwriting. Thai and Tai Tham scripts are documented much later.

periods.title: The polygon vanishes, while language history continues
periods.summary: The 323 BCE snapshot removes the exact feature and repaints sampled points, but no linguistic source records Proto-Tai surrender, extinction, or evacuation then. Tai languages later diversified, interacted, and spread. The ending belongs to atlas classification, not to a people falling off history’s map edge.

sections.title: Start with the label, then test the map

items.text: “Proto-Thai cultures” mixes a reconstructed language ancestor with plural archaeological-sounding cultures. Proto-Tai is not an attested self-name, dynasty, state, or excavated culture. The card therefore uses “Proto-Tai reconstruction and possible communities” and preserves the imported wording only as an atlas alias.

The exact id occurs in one of fifty audited border snapshots. Its single polygon has one ring, twenty-seven positions, and bounds of 102.6244 to 126.9859 degrees east and 34.4079 to 44.1903 degrees north. Precision one is metadata, not a Bronze Age surveyor’s confidence score.

Point tests place Lanzhou and Ordos inside, while Beijing, Tianjin, Shenyang, Jinan, Taiyuan, Xi’an, Nanjing, Changsha, Guiyang, Nanning, Guangzhou, Haikou, and Hanoi all fall outside. The shape therefore plainly misses the southern geography that linguistic scholarship actually discusses in detail.

The polygon shares encoded arcs with atlas features labeled Zhou states, Xiongnu, Proto-Tibetan cultures, and Gojoseon. Those seams reveal how the source map was tiled; they do not prove that Proto-Tai speakers bordered four named peoples along exact frontiers in 400 BCE.

Between the 400 and 323 BCE snapshots, Ordos changes from the exact label to Zhou states, Lanzhou loses a label, and several southern samples also change independently. That many simultaneous edits identify an atlas repaint. No family packed up because a JSON file reached its next date.

Pittayaporn reconstructs Proto-Tai phonology through systematic comparison across modern Tai varieties, while accounting for contact and recurrent sound change. The star before a form marks reconstruction. It means “inferred from evidence,” not “copied from a 2,400-year-old notebook somebody conveniently forgot to preserve.”

Kra-Dai includes several branches; Tai is only one. Hlai, Kra, Kam-Sui, and other lineages matter to deeper family history, and scholars differ over some subgrouping. Calling every ancient Kra-Dai-speaking community “Thai” compresses linguistic diversity and imports a modern national spelling into prehistory.

Modern Tai languages share inherited features yet also reflect convergence and borrowing across mainland Southeast Asia. Similar tones, word orders, or cultural terms can spread through contact. Historical linguists therefore compare regular correspondences across many words rather than declaring cousins whenever two languages happen to sound friendly.

Bayesian language trees offer model-based estimates for early Kra-Dai divergence, but dates depend on data, calibration, sampling, and assumptions. They are probability distributions, not appointment books. Their southern and coastal dispersal results contradict the atlas geometry, yet they do not establish one uncontested homeland.

Chinese loanword layers help date the much later spread of Proto-Southwestern Tai, a descendant branch rather than Proto-Tai itself. That evidence supports later movement from southern China into mainland Southeast Asia. It cannot be back-projected to certify one people, territory, or event between 400 and 323 BCE.

sections.title: Keep language, archaeology, and ancestry in separate evidence boxes

items.text: Lingnan archaeology records changing pottery technologies, settlement patterns, metalworking, and exchange across communities south of the Nanling ranges. Those material patterns deserve their own names and chronologies. Without inscriptions or another independent bridge, a pot cannot tell archaeologists which language its maker spoke.

High-fired proto-porcelain and specialized kiln knowledge moved through Bronze Age Lingnan production and consumption networks. The evidence demonstrates skilled craftspeople and long connections among regions. It does not identify a “Proto-Tai ceramic style,” and technological transfer need not follow a language-family branch.

Dong Son drums, tools, weapons, ornaments, and ceramics illuminate northern Vietnamese Bronze and Iron Age communities. Museums date the broad tradition across the first millennium BCE and later. The objects are regionally relevant comparisons, but assigning every drum to Proto-Tai would replace an archaeological question with a label.

A later Dong Son drum model shows how bronzes could carry ritual, funerary, and political meaning and travel widely. Its later date and tomb context matter. Attractive museum objects are excellent evidence for themselves; they are not decorative passports proving the language of every craftsperson.

Genomic studies reveal repeated migration and admixture among southern Chinese and Southeast Asian populations. Genes can illuminate biological relationships among sampled people, while languages can spread through migration, marriage, trade, power, or language shift. Equating one genetic cluster with Proto-Tai would confuse related but different histories.

sections.title: Farm, fish, weave, make, and exchange with caution

items.text: Rice had a long regional history before the atlas interval, with cultivation and domestication reconstructed through plant remains and genetics. Rice alone cannot identify Proto-Tai speakers: many communities speaking unrelated languages grew it. A grain can reveal species, processing, and diet, but it declines to answer linguistic surveys.

Archaeology across mainland Southeast Asia documents settlements combining cultivation, animal keeping, fishing, gathering, ceramics, and metalwork in varying proportions. Ban Chiang is one important sequence, not a universal village blueprint. Subsistence changed communally through ecology, season, household resources, and exchange.

River corridors and coasts connected Lingnan with neighboring regions through movement of people, knowledge, ceramics, metals, and other goods. Routes created multilingual contact rather than tidy cultural lanes. A traded vessel proves circulation and choice; it does not automatically reveal a merchant’s mother tongue.

The reconstructible Proto-Tai form *tamᴮ means “weave” in modern scholarly notation. It supports ancestral knowledge of weaving, while loom forms, fibers, patterns, and labor arrangements could vary. Language and loom phylogenies partly diverge because technologies can be borrowed, retained, redesigned, or abandoned.

Living Kra-Dai-speaking weavers use multiple loom systems, and some communities trade for cloth rather than weave it. Present variation warns against dressing every Proto-Tai speaker in one imagined outfit. It also shows the achievement hidden in cloth: fiber preparation, tension, counting, pattern memory, repair, and social exchange.

sections.title: Put households, relationships, and gatherings inside the uncertainty

items.text: No reviewed source identifies household size, marriage residence, inheritance, descent rules, or gendered work for Proto-Tai communities during this interval. Reconstructed kin terms may illuminate language history, but they do not automatically map a complete social system. Families also change practice without replacing every word.

Burials and settlements can reveal age, diet, labor, inequality, mobility, and social ties, but regional archaeological assemblages are not securely labeled Proto-Tai. Ban Chiang evidence demonstrates careful cemetery and habitation research. Its modern location in Thailand does not make its ancient residents linguistically Thai.

Archaeologists increasingly analyze gender as relationships and networks rather than assigning every tool to men and every textile to women. That method matters here because the direct evidence is sparse. Fixed job charts would tell us more about a modern storyteller’s assumptions than about ancient households.

In modern Surin weaving communities, women often carry specialist knowledge while households, apprentices, cooperatives, and markets share production. This is valuable living evidence with its own history, not a fossilized Proto-Tai rule. It shows how family work can combine identity, income, ritual, creativity, and change.

Today’s Thai living-heritage inventory includes food, festivals, performance, massage, costume, and craft maintained by distinct communities. Diversity is the lesson. Modern Thai citizens and Tai-language speakers are not one unchanged ancient culture, and continuity never requires every family to practice the same tradition.

sections.title: Let children learn, but do not invent their school day

items.text: Children must have learned speech, movement, food work, safety, social expectations, tools, places, and stories. The reviewed record does not preserve a Proto-Tai school, curriculum, initiation sequence, or universal teaching method for 400 BCE. Observation and participation are plausible; a detailed timetable would be fiction.

Small tools, ornaments, burials, footprints, and changing skeletons can sometimes make children archaeologically visible, yet no such assemblage is securely tied here to Proto-Tai speech. Childhood varied with age, health, status, gender, place, and household. “Ancient child” is not a single job description.

UNESCO projects bring community bearers and teachers together so children learn living heritage through classrooms and local practice. That documents modern safeguarding, not prehistoric schooling. It does show a durable principle: knowledge survives because people teach, practice, question, adapt, and decide that it matters.

No securely dated Proto-Tai inscription or native sentence survives from this interval. The card instead shows *tamᴮ “weave,” a modern reconstruction. The asterisk and tone category are analytical marks; nobody in 400 BCE wrote that form on a classroom board, bronze drum, or grocery list.

The Ram Khamhaeng inscription is traditionally dated 1292 CE, roughly sixteen centuries after this card. UNESCO records its importance and the nomination file acknowledges scholarly authenticity debates. British Library holdings demonstrate still later Thai writing. None supplies Proto-Tai literacy or an invented ancient quotation.

sections.title: Talk about health and care without prescribing imaginary medicine

items.text: People experienced birth, injury, infection, pain, disability, aging, and death, while households necessarily provided care. No reviewed source preserves a Proto-Tai treatment, healer title, drug recipe, diagnosis, or outcome from this interval. A universal herbal cure would be unsupported history and alarmingly adventurous medicine.

Diet, water, smoke, parasites, workload, violence, and social support can leave uneven traces in bodies and settlements. Archaeologists need securely associated remains before estimating disease or care. This card supplies no invented life expectancy, infant mortality rate, epidemic, or medical institution for reconstructed speakers.

A review of ancient Chinese parasites uses rare evidence from mummies, latrines, and burial soil, while stressing the limited sample. That is what responsible health reconstruction looks like: direct material, date, place, and uncertainty. None of those samples is evidence for this proposed Proto-Tai population.

UNESCO documents Nuad Thai as a living traditional-care practice with training and community transmission. It belongs to modern Thai cultural history. Backdating it twenty-four centuries because its present name contains “Thai” would confuse a documented tradition with a reconstructed ancestral language.

Thailand’s modern health system includes public institutions, trained professionals, prevention, treatment, and changing access. This later achievement shows how radically care can transform. It cannot supply missing Iron Age facts, but it keeps “continuity” from pretending that health knowledge and institutions stayed frozen.

sections.title: Follow water and waste, and leave unknown toilets unknown

items.text: Settlements needed drinking water and ways to manage food scraps, ash, broken objects, animal waste, and human waste. The reviewed sources do not identify a Proto-Tai well, drain, latrine, privy, sewer, hygiene tool, or waste pit for this interval. Necessity is not a floor plan.

Rivers enabled farming, fishing, transport, and exchange, while floods, contamination, and seasonal scarcity created risk. Regional geography makes these questions important but cannot reveal one community’s water rules or maintenance work. “They lived near water” is not evidence that everybody enjoyed convenient plumbing.

Ancient parasite research can test latrine sediment, coprolites, and burial soil, sometimes identifying infection and mobility. Those methods also reveal how exceptional preserved toilet evidence is. No comparable sample links this card’s proposed speakers, period, and southern homeland discussion, so the bathroom remains archaeologically unassigned.

A later Han-period latrine far northwest of the proposed homeland preserved cloth-wrapped hygiene sticks and parasite eggs. It is wonderfully direct evidence for that site and travelers. It is not a spare toilet we can move backward and southeast to furnish an imaginary Proto-Tai village.

UNICEF links safe water, usable toilets, hygiene, maintenance, and children’s health. That is modern public-health framing, not evidence for ancient facilities. It helps explain why the card asks about access, privacy, upkeep, disposal, and contamination rather than celebrating any mysterious hole as “probably a toilet.”

sections.title: Recognize achievements without manufacturing a civilization

items.text: Comparative reconstruction itself is an achievement of modern scholarship: regular sound correspondences recover aspects of an unrecorded language from its descendants. The result is a testable model that can change with new data. It should not be mistaken for a complete biography of ancient people.

An ancestral weaving verb supports an important human accomplishment: planning fibers, tension, sequence, and repetition well enough to make cloth. Archaeology and living looms show technological diversity. Credit belongs to generations of craftspeople, while the evidence refuses to issue them one standardized ethnic uniform.

Southern communities mastered rice cultivation, pottery firing, bronze casting, navigation, and exchange in overlapping regional systems. These achievements were shared, borrowed, adapted, and locally transformed. Praising them does not require assigning every innovation to Proto-Tai speakers or pretending one language family invented southern China.

Dong Son bronzes demonstrate sophisticated casting and wide circulation, while their functions and makers varied. Ban Chiang preserves long settlement and craft sequences. These are named archaeological contexts with real evidence. The card honors them best by resisting the urge to relabel both as one “Proto-Thai civilization.”

Kra-Dai languages and communities persist across southern China and Southeast Asia through immense diversity and change. Later texts, scripts, arts, states, migrations, and living heritage deserve their own dates and names. Continuity is a branching history, not an unbroken costume parade marching out of 400 BCE.

sections.title: End the atlas interval without ending the people

items.text: Nothing in the reviewed linguistic or archaeological sources makes 323 BCE the death of Proto-Tai, a conquest of its speakers, or the abandonment of a homeland. The date is the next atlas snapshot. A missing polygon is a cartographic event until independent evidence proves more.

The feature’s disappearance accompanies repaints affecting north-China and southern sample points, while its geometry had already contradicted linguistic geography. The safest conclusion is removal of a mistaken layer. The data defect is historically informative because it shows exactly why maps need identity, chronology, and border audits.

Loanword chronology places major Proto-Southwestern Tai dispersal much later than this interval. Later Tai-speaking societies formed across present China, Vietnam, Laos, Thailand, Myanmar, and India through migration, contact, language shift, and local history. None is a frozen remnant of one 400 BCE culture.

Proposals linking Kra-Dai with Austronesian remain scholarly hypotheses evaluated through correspondences and competing models. Even if a deeper relationship gains support, it would not identify this polygon, its dates, or one archaeological culture. Family trees answer ancestry questions; they do not automatically draw maps.

Future discoveries could improve dates, vocabulary, archaeology, ancient DNA, or links among evidence types. A strong card leaves room for revision. For now, it preserves the exact id for navigation, corrects its meaning, records the geometry error, and connects readers to evidence instead of filling silence with certainty.

ending.text: The exact “proto-thai-cultures” feature disappears in the 323 BCE snapshot, but the reviewed evidence supplies no corresponding defeat, migration, political collapse, language death, or population disappearance. The map had placed its only polygon across north China, far from the southern geography emphasized by Kra-Dai research. Its removal is therefore best treated as an atlas repaint correcting or replacing a weak classification. Proto-Tai remains a comparative reconstruction from later Tai languages, not a polity with a recorded final year. Archaeological communities across southern China and mainland Southeast Asia continued farming, fishing, making pottery and metal objects, weaving, trading, raising children, caring for illness, and managing water in locally varied ways; assigning all of them to one language would still exceed the evidence. Much later, Tai branches spread and diversified through migration and contact, and communities created scripts, states, literatures, arts, and living traditions. The card assigns no automatic predecessor or successor. What ends in 323 BCE is one inaccurate polygon, not human continuity.
